issues.legal_issue: A land lease permitting construction of houses or other uses is not within a rent-protection definition limited to land let principally for business or trade unless that principal commercial purpose is established.
material_facts: The land was leased separately, with permission to construct houses or to use the land in any manner.
The lease did not establish that the land was let principally for business or trade, even though buildings were later constructed and some were rented out.
In an execution proceeding, the occupants challenged the consent decree for possession as contrary to the rent restriction law.
issues.conclusion: The land was not within the statutory definition of premises, so the rent restriction law did not apply and the consent decree was not invalid on that ground.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 4(2)(b) of the Bombay Rent Restriction Act, 1939, separately let land falls within the definition of premises only when it is let principally for business or trade. A lease merely permitting construction of houses, or other use of the land, does not itself establish that principal purpose. The court did not rely on any earlier case for this issue.

predicates.execution_challenge: Occupants challenged a decree for possession in an execution proceeding on the ground that rent protection applied.
predicates.separately_leased_land: The lessor leased land separately rather than leasing a building or part of a building.
predicates.lease_not_principally_commercial: The lease permitted construction of houses or other uses but did not establish that the land was to be used principally for business or trade.

issues.definition: When occupants challenge a possession decree in execution, separately leased land that was not let principally for business or trade does not make the decree invalid under rent protection.

issues.legal_issue: A consent decree allowing occupants to remain temporarily after they became liable to eviction does not create a new tenancy when its terms grant only a concession in return for mesne profits.
material_facts: The occupants were liable to immediate eviction after the lease ended.
The consent decree allowed them to remain in possession for five years as a concession and required payment of mesne profits at a substantially higher rate than the original rent.
The decree required the mesne profits to be paid within a shorter period than the period of continued possession and allowed possession to be demanded immediately upon default.
The occupants argued in an execution proceeding that the consent decree created a tenancy protected by later rent-control legislation.
issues.conclusion: The consent decree did not create a tenancy, and the occupants were not protected from eviction on that basis.
issues.legal_principle: The terms of the consent decree must show an intention to create a landlord-and-tenant relationship; temporary continued possession in return for mesne profits is not enough. The court distinguished Gurupadappa, Shivlingappa Itgi v. Sayad Akbar Sayad Budan Kadri, where the consent decree expressly recognized the occupant as a monthly tenant. The court considered the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, but identified no particular provision of that Act as the basis for its conclusion.

rule.if: execution_challenge and occupants_were_liable_to_eviction and decree_granted_temporary_possession and decree_required_mesne_profits

predicates.execution_challenge: Occupants argued in an execution proceeding that a consent decree protected them from eviction.
predicates.occupants_were_liable_to_eviction: The occupants were liable to be evicted when the prior lease ended.
predicates.decree_granted_temporary_possession: The decree allowed the occupants to remain in possession temporarily as a concession rather than recognizing an ongoing tenancy.
predicates.decree_required_mesne_profits: The decree required the occupants to pay mesne profits for the period of temporary possession.

issues.definition: When occupants liable to eviction receive only temporary possession under a decree in return for mesne profits, that decree does not create a tenancy.

issues.legal_issue: More than one decree may be passed at different stages in the same suit when a compromise resolves part of the suit and the remaining defendants' rights are decided later.
material_facts: A single suit sought possession from multiple occupants.
A consent decree was passed after some defendants compromised, and a later separate consent decree resolved the claims against the remaining defendants.
The occupants challenged the decrees in execution on the ground that the court could pass only one decree in the suit.
issues.conclusion: The court was competent to pass separate decrees at different stages in the same suit, and neither decree was a nullity.
issues.legal_principle: Order XXIII rule 3 of the Code of Civil Procedure contemplates a decree on compromise for part of the subject matter, and Order XII rule 6 permits judgment at any stage. These provisions allow more than one decree in the same suit at different stages; the provisions of Order XX rules 1 and 12 relied upon by the appellants did not prevent that result. No earlier case was relied on for this issue.

predicates.execution_challenge: Occupants challenged the validity of decrees in an execution proceeding.
predicates.one_suit_involved_multiple_defendant_gro: A single suit sought relief against multiple groups of defendants.
predicates.decree_resolved_one_group_before_another: The court entered a decree resolving one group of defendants' claims before resolving the claims against another group.

issues.definition: When one suit against multiple defendant groups is resolved in stages, separate decrees for those stages are valid.
